patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.complaint: Blurred vision in the right eye for 4 days, with pain when moving the eye
background: Two years ago: numbness and tingling in both legs for 3 weeks that settled on its own
No other medical history; takes no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young woman, subacute painful monocular visual loss, red desaturation, a central scotoma and an RAPD. Finding questions ask for the field defect, the pupil sign or the fundus.

points: Priya, 28, noticed her right eye was 'foggy' 4 days ago.
It has slowly got worse over days.
It **aches when she looks around**, especially side to side.
Red things look **washed out** through the right eye.

steps.lead: Priya's right optic nerve is inflamed, so only the **right eye** loses vision. In a young woman, think **MS** first.
Priya fits the typical patient: a **young woman** with **subacute, one-eyed** visual loss.

points: Ishihara: right 5 of 17 plates; left 17 of 17.
Visual fields: a **central blind spot** in the right eye.

steps.lead: Every feature fits: **pain on eye movement**, blurred vision, **red desaturation**, low Ishihara score and a **central scotoma**.

visual.label: Priya 5/17

steps.q: A torch swings from Priya's left eye to her right. Her right pupil appears to dilate. What is this?
steps.r: A **RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil)**: the damaged right optic nerve carries a weaker light signal, so both pupils relax when the light moves to it.

steps.lead: Priya has the signature **right RAPD** with a **normal-looking disc** (retrobulbar). Months later the disc may turn **pale**.
Priya has no headache, no slow onset and one eye only. **NMO** would be bilateral, faster, with long cord lesions and **anti-aquaporin-4** antibodies.
Priya's leg tingling 2 years ago is a red flag: **40–70%** with optic neuritis develop or already have **MS**.

steps.text: Do not call a swollen disc 'papilloedema' here. **Papilloedema** means disc swelling from **raised ICP** and is usually bilateral; optic neuritis swelling is inflammatory.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' with the answer MRI brain and orbits plus whole spine with contrast, looking for demyelinating plaques. Bedside tests are colour vision and visual fields.

visual.label: Priya 6/36

steps.title: Priya's results
steps.text: Enhancing optic nerve with **periventricular plaques**: optic neuritis with a high MS risk. Normal ESR and pressure argue against GCA and glaucoma.

steps.lead: Priya's right optic nerve has **inflammatory demyelination**, most often the first sign of MS.
Losing myelin slows Priya's nerve conduction: **colour vision** suffers first, then acuity, with a central scotoma.
Priya's eye hurts on movement because the **inflamed nerve sheath** is tethered to the eye muscles and gets stretched.

nodes: Light into healthy left eye: strong afferent signal
Light swings to right eye: weak afferent signal
Less constriction, so both pupils relax

Priya's steroids reduce **inflammation and oedema**, so she recovers faster, but her final vision and MS risk are unchanged.

prompts.q: What is optic neuritis, who gets it and what is the most common cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: young woman + one eye + days = optic neuritis.

points.p: Inflammation of the optic nerve; ipsilateral visual loss
points.why: A lesion before the chiasm affects only that eye.

points.p: Most common cause: multiple sclerosis
points.why: Often the first sign of MS.

points.p: Young females
points.why: Older patients make ischaemic causes more likely.

points.p: Subacute unilateral (monocular) visual loss
points.why: Sudden loss suggests ischaemia; bilateral suggests NMO or nutritional.

prompts.q: Describe the presentation of optic neuritis, including the field defect and colour vision.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pain on movement and red desaturation are the giveaways.

points.p: Eye pain worse on movement
points.why: Ischaemic optic neuropathy gives headache instead.

points.p: Blurred vision in one eye, reduced acuity
points.why: Acuity can range from near normal to severe.

points.p: Red desaturation, reduced Ishihara scores
points.why: Colour vision is particularly sensitive.

points.p: Central scotoma (most common field defect)
points.why: Bitemporal hemianopia means the chiasm, not the nerve.

points.p: Photopsia (flashing lights), other field defects
points.why: Flashes alone with floaters suggest retinal detachment.

prompts.q: What is the signature examination finding, and what does the fundus show early and late?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a normal fundus does not exclude optic neuritis.

points.p: RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil on swinging light test
points.why: Affected pupil appears relatively dilated.

points.p: Fundoscopy often normal early
points.why: Retrobulbar inflammation is behind the visible disc.

points.p: Acute disc swelling; chronically optic atrophy (pale disc)
points.why: Pallor is the late finding.

points.p: Papilloedema is disc swelling from raised ICP specifically
points.why: Do not use the word papilloedema for optic neuritis.

prompts.q: How do you tell optic neuritis from ischaemic, compressive and nutritional optic neuropathies?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: onset, pain and laterality separate them.

points.p: Ischaemic (e.g. GCA): headache not pain on movement, more acute
points.why: Check ESR/CRP in older patients.

points.p: Compressive (glioma, metastasis): insidious, rarely painful
points.why: Slow progression is the clue.

points.p: Nutritional (B12/folate, alcohol): bilateral, symmetrical, no RAPD
points.why: Symmetrical loss gives no relative defect.

points.p: Others: raised ICP, malignant hypertension, sarcoidosis, ethambutol
points.why: Ethambutol needs acuity and colour monitoring.

prompts.q: What are the complications of optic neuritis, and what features suggest neuromyelitis optica?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bilateral optic neuritis plus a long cord lesion = NMO.

points.p: 40–70% develop or have MS
points.why: The biggest long-term association.

points.p: Persistent visual deficit, recurrence, colour vision impairment
points.why: Colour deficits often persist.

points.p: NMO: bilateral, quicker onset, longitudinally extensive cord lesions
points.why: Plus bladder dysfunction and leg weakness.

points.p: Anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies
points.why: Distinguishes NMO from MS.

prompts.q: How is optic neuritis investigated? Name the key scan and bedside tests.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: MRI with contrast, never CT.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis plus MRI; refer all to neurology
points.why: May be the first sign of MS.

points.p: MRI brain and orbits plus whole spine with contrast
points.why: Looks for demyelinating plaques suggesting MS.

points.p: Visual field and colour vision testing
points.why: Documents the central scotoma and red desaturation.

points.p: Specialist: OCT and VEP
points.why: VEPs show delayed conduction.

prompts.q: Which mimics must be excluded in suspected optic neuritis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a red eye or high pressure means it is not optic neuritis.

points.p: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
points.why: Red painful eye, high pressure, haloes.

points.p: Retinal detachment
points.why: Flashes, floaters, curtain.

points.p: Uveitis
points.why: Red eye with photophobia.

points.p: Stroke or other visual pathway lesion
points.why: Field defects affect both eyes.

prompts.q: How is acute optic neuritis treated, and what is the long-term plan?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: IV first, then oral taper; and follow up for MS.

points.p: IV methylprednisolone, then oral prednisolone taper
points.why: Standard acute treatment.

points.p: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics before treating
points.why: Steroids could harm an infective cause.

points.p: If MRI shows demyelination, assess MS risk
points.why: Neurology decide on disease-modifying treatment.

points.p: Ongoing ophthalmology and neurology follow-up
points.why: May be the first sign of MS.

prompts.q: Explain why optic neuritis reduces colour vision, hurts on eye movement and causes an RAPD.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link each sign to demyelination of one nerve.

points.p: Inflammatory demyelination slows or blocks conduction; colour vision particularly sensitive
points.why: Explains acuity loss and the scotoma.

points.p: Inflamed nerve sheath tethered to extraocular muscles is stretched on movement
points.why: Hence pain on movement, not at rest.

points.p: Reduced afferent conduction: light in affected eye gives weaker constriction
points.why: The efferent (CN III) side is normal.

prompts.q: How does NMO differ from MS-related optic neuritis, and why are steroids given?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: steroids change speed, not outcome.

points.p: NMO: anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies against astrocytes
points.why: More severe, bilateral, longitudinally extensive.

points.p: Steroids reduce inflammation and oedema, accelerating recovery
points.why: Supported by the ONTT.

points.p: Do not change long-term vision or MS conversion risk
points.why: A classic SBA trap.

glossary.optic neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve, causing painful loss of vision in one eye.
glossary.optic nerve: Cranial nerve II, carrying visual signals from the retina to the brain.
glossary.multiple sclerosis: Immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the brain and spinal cord with episodes separated in time and space.
glossary.demyelination: Loss of the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, slowing or blocking conduction.
glossary.subacute: Developing over days, not seconds or months.
glossary.red desaturation: Red objects appear faded or washed out in the affected eye.
glossary.Ishihara: Colour vision test using plates of coloured dots containing hidden numbers.
glossary.central scotoma: A blind or dim spot in the centre of the visual field.
glossary.scotoma: An area of lost or reduced vision within the visual field.
glossary.RAPD: Relative afferent pupillary defect: the affected pupil dilates when the light swings to it.
glossary.Marcus Gunn pupil: Another name for a relative afferent pupillary defect.
glossary.swinging light test: Moving a torch between the eyes to compare each optic nerve's pupil response.
glossary.consensual reflex: Constriction of one pupil when light is shone into the other eye.
glossary.fundoscopy: Looking at the retina and optic disc with an ophthalmoscope.
glossary.retrobulbar: Behind the eyeball; retrobulbar optic neuritis leaves the disc looking normal.
glossary.optic atrophy: Pale optic disc from loss of nerve fibres, a late sign after optic neuritis.
glossary.papilloedema: Optic disc swelling caused specifically by raised intracranial pressure.
glossary.ischaemic optic neuropathy: Optic nerve damage from poor blood supply, e.g. in giant cell arteritis.
glossary.GCA: Giant cell arteritis: large-vessel vasculitis in older people causing headache and sudden visual loss.
glossary.ethambutol: TB drug that can cause optic neuropathy; acuity and colour vision need monitoring.
glossary.neuromyelitis optica: Antibody-mediated disease causing severe optic neuritis and long spinal cord lesions.
glossary.aquaporin-4: Water channel on astrocytes; antibodies against it cause neuromyelitis optica.
glossary.astrocytes: Supporting glial cells of the central nervous system.
glossary.longitudinally extensive: A spinal cord lesion spanning three or more vertebral segments, typical of NMO.
glossary.periventricular: Next to the brain's ventricles; a classic site for MS plaques.
glossary.OCT: Optical coherence tomography: scan measuring retinal nerve fibre layer thickness.
glossary.VEP: Visual evoked potentials: measures conduction time along the visual pathway; delayed in demyelination.
glossary.methylprednisolone: High-dose intravenous corticosteroid used for acute optic neuritis and MS relapses.
glossary.prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid used to taper after IV methylprednisolone.
glossary.ONTT: Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial: showed steroids speed recovery but do not change final vision.
glossary.LogMAR: Visual acuity scale where 0.0 is normal and higher numbers mean worse vision.
glossary.Snellen: Letter chart acuity, e.g. 6/6 normal, 6/36 reduced.
glossary.acute angle-closure glaucoma: Sudden rise in eye pressure causing a red, painful eye, haloes and vomiting.
glossary.uveitis: Inflammation of the iris, ciliary body or choroid, causing a red, photophobic eye.
glossary.retinal detachment: Separation of the retina, causing flashes, floaters and a curtain over vision.
glossary.bitemporal hemianopia: Loss of both outer visual fields, from a chiasm lesion such as a pituitary tumour.
glossary.extraocular muscles: The six muscles that move the eye.

technique.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 5 day history of blurred vision in her left eye that has worsened over several days. It hurts when she moves her eyes. Colours look faded through the left eye. Visual acuity is 6/24 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right. On the swinging light test the left pupil dilates when the light is moved to it. The left fundus is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about monocular visual loss.

clues: hurts when she moves her eyes
left pupil dilates when the light is moved to it
steps.x: Young woman, subacute, **pain on movement**, red desaturation, **RAPD**, normal disc.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Optic neuritis**, retrobulbar.

elim: Angle closure gives a red, very painful eye with haloes and high pressure.
Ischaemic optic neuropathy affects older people, is painless or with headache and more acute.
CRAO is sudden and painless with a pale retina and cherry-red spot.
Detachment gives flashes, floaters and a curtain, not pain on movement.

steps.x: **D. Optic neuritis.** Young + days + pain on movement + RAPD = optic neuritis.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 1 week history of painful loss of vision in her right eye. She has reduced colour vision and a central scotoma in that eye, with a right relative afferent pupillary defect. A year ago she had an episode of numbness in her left arm that resolved. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to look for an underlying cause?
o: MRI brain, orbits and whole spine with contrast

steps.x: The underlying cause: you are looking for MS.

clues: painful loss of vision in her right eye
numbness in her left arm that resolved
steps.x: Optic neuritis plus a previous neurological episode: likely **MS**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI brain, orbits and whole spine with contrast** for demyelinating plaques.

elim: CT cannot show demyelinating plaques.
ESR is for suspected GCA in older people.
LP for oligoclonal bands is supportive, not first-line.
VEPs are a specialist add-on, not the key test.

steps.x: **D. MRI with contrast.** Clinical diagnosis + MRI; refer to neurology.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has been treated for right optic neuritis with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone. Her vision is improving. MRI brain shows several periventricular white matter lesions. She has no current limb symptoms. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Neurology follow-up to assess multiple sclerosis risk

steps.x: Long-term step after the acute episode.
Demyelinating lesions on MRI mean a **high MS risk**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Neurology follow-up** to assess MS risk.

elim: This may be the first sign of MS; she needs follow-up.
Long-term steroids do not change MS risk and cause harm.
Plasma exchange is for severe steroid-refractory cases.
Steroids do not alter conversion to MS.

steps.x: **C. Neurology follow-up for MS risk.** Plaques on MRI change the long-term plan.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has optic neuritis in his left eye. When a light is shone into his right eye, both pupils constrict briskly. When the light is swung quickly to the left eye, both pupils dilate slightly.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this finding?
o: Damage to the left oculomotor nerve
Reduced afferent conduction in the left optic nerve

steps.x: Explain an RAPD mechanistically.

clues: optic neuritis in his left eye
steps.x: Both pupils move together, so the efferent side is fine; the left input signal is weaker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reduced afferent conduction** in the left optic nerve.

elim: CN III damage is efferent: that pupil would not constrict at all.
Iris damage would affect only one pupil.
Sympathetic lesions cause Horner's (small pupil, ptosis).
Tectal lesions cause light-near dissociation in both eyes.

steps.x: **C. Reduced afferent conduction.** RAPD = afferent problem in the affected eye.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has a 4 day history of blurred vision in her right eye, with an ache behind the eye that is worse when she looks to the side. Visual acuity is 6/18 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. The eye is white. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Subacute painful monocular visual loss worse on eye movement in a young woman with a white eye and normal pressure is optic neuritis. GCA occurs in older people with a raised ESR.

steps.x: Diagnosis of painful monocular visual loss.

clues: worse when she looks to the side
steps.x: Young woman, days, **pain on movement**, quiet eye, normal pressure and ESR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Optic neuritis**.

elim: Angle closure gives a red eye and high pressure; pressure is 16.
Uveitis gives a red, photophobic eye.
CRAO is sudden and painless with a pale retina.
GCA affects over 50s and the ESR is normal.

steps.x: **E. Optic neuritis.** White eye + pain on movement + young = optic neuritis.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 1 week history of painful blurred vision in her left eye. Colours look washed out. On examination there is a left relative afferent pupillary defect and the left optic disc looks normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on visual field testing?
practice.e: A central scotoma is the most common visual field defect in optic neuritis. Bitemporal and homonymous defects arise from the chiasm and beyond and affect both eyes.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question on fields.

clues: painful blurred vision in her left eye
steps.x: Classic optic neuritis of one nerve.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Central scotoma**.

elim: Bitemporal hemianopia means a chiasmal lesion.
Altitudinal defects are typical of ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Homonymous defects are post-chiasmal and affect both eyes.
Peripheral constriction suggests glaucoma or retinitis pigmentosa.

steps.x: **B. Central scotoma.** The most common field defect in optic neuritis.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has had painful, reduced vision in his left eye for 6 days. Pain is worse on eye movement and he has red desaturation in the left eye. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. A torch is swung between his eyes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the swinging light test?
o: Left fixed dilated pupil with ptosis
practice.e: An affected left optic nerve gives a left RAPD: the left pupil appears to dilate when the light moves to it. A fixed dilated pupil with ptosis is a third nerve palsy.

steps.x: Pupil finding in optic neuritis: which side?

clues: reduced vision in his left eye
red desaturation in the left eye
steps.x: Left optic neuritis: the **left** afferent pathway is damaged.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left RAPD**.

elim: Light-near dissociation is a midbrain or Argyll Robertson sign.
That is a third nerve palsy.
The RAPD is on the side of the affected nerve.
That is Horner's syndrome.

steps.x: **C. Left RAPD.** The RAPD sits on the side of the inflamed nerve.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has optic neuritis in her right eye. Eighteen months ago she had 2 weeks of tingling in both legs and urinary urgency, which resolved. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. MRI brain shows periventricular white matter lesions; the spinal cord shows a short lesion spanning one segment.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her optic neuritis?
practice.e: Two neurological episodes separated in time and space with periventricular plaques and a short cord lesion is MS, the most common cause of optic neuritis. NMO gives longitudinally extensive lesions and anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies.

steps.x: The underlying cause of optic neuritis.

clues: tingling in both legs and urinary urgency, which resolved
steps.x: Relapsing episodes, periventricular plaques, a **short** cord lesion, AQP4 negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Multiple sclerosis**.

elim: GCA affects older people and gives ischaemic, not inflammatory, neuropathy.
NMO gives longitudinally extensive cord lesions and AQP4 antibodies; hers is negative.
Sarcoid would give systemic features such as hilar lymphadenopathy.
B12 deficiency gives bilateral symmetrical loss without RAPD.

steps.x: **B. Multiple sclerosis.** MS is the most common cause of optic neuritis.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has had 3 days of reduced vision in her right eye with pain on looking around. Acuity is 6/36 in the right eye. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on fundoscopy of the right eye?
o: Retinal tear with a grey elevated retina
practice.e: Fundoscopy is often normal early in optic neuritis because the inflammation is retrobulbar; disc pallor appears later. A cherry-red spot is CRAO and widespread haemorrhages are CRVO.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' on fundoscopy, early in the illness.
Early optic neuritis: often **retrobulbar**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Normal optic disc**.

elim: Cherry-red spot means central retinal artery occlusion.
Cupping is glaucoma.
Widespread haemorrhages mean central retinal vein occlusion.
A grey elevated retina is a detachment.

steps.x: **C. Normal optic disc.** Early optic neuritis: 'the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing'.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman had an episode of painful visual loss in her left eye 8 months ago, which mostly recovered. Her left eye acuity is now 6/9, and red objects still look duller in that eye. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Fundoscopy is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on fundoscopy of the left eye?
o: Pigment clumps in the peripheral retina
practice.e: After optic neuritis the disc becomes pale (optic atrophy) as nerve fibres are lost, with lasting colour impairment. Bilateral swollen discs would be papilloedema from raised ICP.

steps.x: A late fundus finding after optic neuritis.

clues: painful visual loss in her left eye 8 months ago
steps.x: Old optic neuritis with persistent colour deficit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronically, **optic atrophy**: a pale disc.

elim: Bilateral disc swelling is papilloedema from raised ICP.
Cotton wool spots suggest hypertension or diabetes.
Drusen suggest macular degeneration.
Peripheral pigment suggests retinitis pigmentosa.

steps.x: **D. Pale optic disc.** Optic atrophy is the late sign.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 5 day history of painful blurred vision in her right eye with red desaturation and a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. She is referred to neurology.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging?
o: MRI brain, orbits and whole spine with contrast
practice.e: MRI of the brain and orbits plus whole spine with contrast looks for demyelinating plaques suggesting MS. CT does not show demyelination.

steps.x: Imaging choice in optic neuritis.

clues: painful blurred vision in her right eye
steps.x: Optic neuritis: the scan must show **demyelination**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI with contrast**.

elim: CT cannot show demyelinating plaques.
CT orbits is for orbital cellulitis or trauma.
Ultrasound does not image the nerve or brain.
Plain films are for fractures and foreign bodies.

steps.x: **C. MRI brain, orbits and whole spine with contrast.**

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman reports that her right eye has become blurry over 3 days, with pain on eye movement. Visual acuity is 6/9 in the right eye, only mildly reduced. The GP wants a quick bedside test of optic nerve function. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which bedside test is most likely to be abnormal?
practice.e: Colour vision is particularly sensitive in optic neuritis, so Ishihara plates are often abnormal even when acuity is near normal. Amsler grids test the macula; fluorescein tests the cornea.

steps.x: Which simple test detects optic nerve dysfunction?
Optic neuritis with near-normal acuity: colour drops first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ishihara colour plates**.

elim: Amsler grid tests macular distortion.
Fluorescein shows corneal abrasions and ulcers.
Schirmer's measures tear production.
Tonometry measures eye pressure (glaucoma).

steps.x: **C. Ishihara plates.** Red desaturation is an early, sensitive sign.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 1 week history of painful loss of vision in her left eye. Acuity is 6/60. She has a left relative afferent pupillary defect and a central scotoma. MRI shows an enhancing left optic nerve. Mimics have been excluded. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone
practice.e: IV methylprednisolone tapered with oral prednisolone is the standard acute treatment of optic neuritis. Topical drops do not reach the optic nerve; plasma exchange is reserved for severe refractory cases.

steps.x: Acute treatment of confirmed optic neuritis.
Diagnosis confirmed, mimics excluded, severe visual loss.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman sees her GP with a 3 day history of blurred vision in her right eye and pain when moving the eye. Acuity is 6/24 in the right eye with red desaturation. She is otherwise well. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Oral prednisolone started by the GP
Urgent same-day referral to ophthalmology or neurology
practice.e: All suspected optic neuritis needs urgent specialist assessment to confirm the diagnosis, exclude mimics and arrange MRI. Oral steroids alone from the GP are not standard treatment.

steps.x: **E. Urgent same-day specialist referral.** Confirm and exclude mimics before treating.

practice.stem: A 27 year old man with right optic neuritis is offered intravenous methylprednisolone. He asks whether the treatment will improve how well he can see in a year's time or stop him getting multiple sclerosis. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most accurate advice about the steroid treatment?
o: Faster visual recovery, with no change in final vision or MS risk
It cures the underlying multiple sclerosis
It improves final vision and reduces MS risk
It is needed to prevent permanent blindness in all cases
practice.e: Steroids reduce inflammation and oedema, accelerating visual recovery, but do not alter long-term visual outcome or MS conversion risk (ONTT).

steps.x: **A. Faster recovery only.** Steroids change speed, not outcome.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has left optic neuritis. She has a dull ache behind the left eye at rest that becomes sharp when she looks up or to the side. The eye is white and intraocular pressure is normal. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the pain on eye movement?
o: Stretching of the inflamed optic nerve sheath by the extraocular muscles
Trigeminal nerve compression in the cavernous sinus
practice.e: The inflamed optic nerve sheath is tethered to the extraocular muscles and orbital fascia, so eye movement stretches it. Raised pressure and ciliary inflammation are excluded by a white eye with normal pressure.

steps.x: Mechanism of pain on eye movement.

clues: sharp when she looks up or to the side
steps.x: Pain triggered by **movement** with a quiet eye.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **inflamed sheath is tethered** to the eye muscles and stretched.

elim: Corneal damage gives a red, gritty eye.
Ciliary inflammation (uveitis) gives a red, photophobic eye.
Pressure is normal.
Cavernous sinus lesions cause ophthalmoplegia and facial numbness.

steps.x: **D. Stretching of the inflamed nerve sheath.**
